profile.title: Professor, P.Eng.
profile.heroAlt: Professor Fitsum Tariku with Building Science graduates Alden Kung, Rocky Tam, and Luke King
profile.statement: How buildings can stay durable, low-carbon, and comfortable as the climate changes.
profile.summary: The lab studies materials, envelopes, and whole buildings with experiments and computer models. The aim is practical guidance for net-zero design, and for buildings that remain healthy in hotter, wetter weather.
bio: Fitsum Tariku is a professor in the School of Sustainable Energy Engineering at Simon Fraser University. He joined SFU in May 2025 to build a building engineering physics group. His work joins laboratory measurements with models of heat, air, and moisture, from a single material up to a whole building in a city.

Before SFU he was at the British Columbia Institute of Technology, where he held a Canada Research Chair in whole-building performance and founded the Building Science master's programs. He is a professional engineer. He earned his PhD in Building Engineering at Concordia University, his master's in Mechanical Engineering at the University of New Brunswick, and his bachelor's at Addis Ababa University.

research.title: Low-carbon materials
research.teaser: Materials that cut carbon without failing in heat or moisture.
research.summary: Measuring and modeling materials that cut the carbon of construction without giving up thermal or moisture performance. Recent work includes hempcrete in mild and cold climates, aging of roof insulation, and a Canada Foundation for Innovation project on low-carbon materials for net-zero buildings. A U.S. patent application for an aerogel-enhanced bio-based material was filed in 2023.

research.title: High-performance envelopes
research.teaser: Walls and roofs that save energy and still dry out.
research.summary: How walls and roofs move heat, air, and moisture in real weather. The group studies rainscreen cavities, ventilated walls, thermal bridges, highly insulated assemblies, and green roofs on insulated decks. The goal is envelopes that save energy and still dry out.

research.title: Whole-building performance
research.teaser: Energy, durability, and comfort treated as one problem.
research.summary: Connecting the envelope, the indoor environment, and building systems. Projects look at energy use, durability, humidity, and the rising risk of overheating. The lab treats comfort and health as part of performance, not as a check after the energy model is finished.

research.title: Urban physics and renewables
research.teaser: Wind, urban heat, and solar built into the envelope.
research.summary: Wind, urban heat, and solar systems built into the envelope. Work includes canopy wind models, urban canopy temperature for energy simulation, and air-based building-integrated photovoltaic/thermal collectors. The question is how a building behaves on a real street, not as an isolated box.

news.title: CFI support for low-carbon materials research
news.summary: The Canada Foundation for Innovation awarded John R. Evans Leaders Fund support for a project on low-carbon building materials for net-zero buildings. The award helps equip the lab's materials research at SFU.

news.title: Professor Tariku joins Sustainable Energy Engineering
news.summary: He joined the School of Sustainable Energy Engineering in May 2025 to establish a building engineering physics research group, and to train engineers for low-carbon, climate-ready buildings.
